lead: An orthogonal set is complete on an interval when adding more of its members drives the error energy of the approximation to zero, for every finite-energy signal on that interval. The signal then equals its orthogonal expansion, x = Σ cₙφₙ, and its energy splits exactly among the terms: E = Σ |cₙ|²Kₙ. That is Parseval's relation. The Fourier series is the most used complete set. Parseval gives the energy or power in each harmonic without a fresh integral.
prereq: You need the inner product, Kₙ and the coefficient formula cₙ = ⟨x, φₙ⟩/Kₙ from Chapter 1.7, and the energy and power of a signal from Chapter 1.2.

sections.h3: Error energy as terms are added

blocks.text: Approximate x(t) on [a, b] by the first N terms of an orthogonal set, Σ cₙφₙ(t) for n = 1 to N, with cₙ = ⟨x, φₙ⟩/Kₙ. Expand the error energy ε(N). Every cross term ⟨φₘ, φₙ⟩ with m ≠ n vanishes, and what is left is short.

ε(N) = ∫ₐᵇ |x(t) − Σ cₙφₙ(t)|² dt
     = ∫ₐᵇ |x(t)|² dt − Σ |cₙ|² Kₙ        (n = 1 to N)
blocks.where: ε(N) is the error energy left after N terms; ∫|x(t)|² dt is the energy E of x on [a, b]; |cₙ|²Kₙ is the energy carried by the n-th term.

items: Each new term lowers the error energy by |cₙ|²Kₙ and can never raise it.
Adding a term does not change the coefficients already found, because each cₙ is one inner product with its own φₙ. This is called the finality of coefficients.
Since ε(N) ≥ 0, Σ |cₙ|²Kₙ ≤ E for every N. This is Bessel's inequality: the terms can never carry more energy than the signal has.

blocks.text: The set {φₙ} is complete on [a, b] when ε(N) → 0 as N → ∞ for every signal of finite energy on [a, b]. An equivalent test: no nonzero finite-energy signal is orthogonal to every member of the set. For a complete set we write x(t) = Σ cₙφₙ(t), the generalised Fourier series of x.
The equality holds in energy. The two sides may still differ at isolated points: at the jump of a square wave a Fourier series gives the midpoint of the jump, but no energy is lost at a single point.

head: Complete set
Interval
Kₙ (energy of each member)
rows: 1, cos nω₀t, sin nω₀t (n = 1, 2, …): trigonometric Fourier series
T₀ for the constant 1; T₀/2 for each cosine and sine

blocks.text: Completeness belongs to the set, not to one signal. The sines {sin nt} on (0, 2π) represent the odd square wave of the worked example exactly, yet they are not complete there: cos t is orthogonal to every sin nt on (0, 2π), so all its sine coefficients are zero. Add the constant and the cosines and the set becomes complete.
For a complete set the error energy reaches zero, so the energy of x equals the sum of the energies of its components.

blocks.where: the sum runs over every member of the set. For an orthonormal set (every Kₙ = 1) it reads E = Σ |cₙ|², the signal version of Pythagoras' theorem.

blocks.text: For a periodic signal, divide both sides by T₀ to get average power. With the exponential set Kₙ = T₀, so P = (1/T₀) ∫ |x(t)|² dt = Σ |Dₙ|², summed over n = 0, ±1, ±2, …, where Dₙ are the exponential Fourier coefficients. With the trigonometric form x(t) = a₀ + Σ (aₙ cos nω₀t + bₙ sin nω₀t) it becomes P = a₀² + Σ (aₙ² + bₙ²)/2.

Check with Chapter 1.2: x(t) = 6 cos(200πt) + 3 has a₀ = 3 and a₁ = 6, so P = 3² + 6²/2 = 9 + 18 = 27 W, the value found there from the time signal. The power spectrum in Parseval's theorem, energy and power spectrum, rests on this relation.

figure.caption: Top: three terms of the sine set already follow the square wave closely. Bottom: the share of its energy 2π that the kept terms carry, from the worked example’s table; the shares rise towards 100 %, as completeness and Parseval’s relation promise.

spec.aria: Top: a square wave with the three-term sine sum wiggling around it. Bottom: five bars of energy share, 81.06, 90.06, 93.31, 94.96 and 95.96 percent, for 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 odd harmonics.

examples.question: The square wave f(t) = 1 for 0 < t < π and f(t) = −1 for π < t < 2π is expanded in sin nt, n = 1, 2, 3, …, on (0, 2π). (a) Find cₙ. (b) Tabulate the energy carried by the terms up to n = 9 and the error energy left. (c) How many nonzero terms carry 90 % of the energy? (d) Verify Parseval's relation, using Σ 1/n² = π²/8 over odd n.
steps: Kₙ = ∫ sin² nt dt over (0, 2π) = π for every n ≥ 1. The energy of f is E = ∫ 1 dt = 2π ≈ 6.283.
⟨f, sin nt⟩ = ∫ sin nt dt over (0, π) − ∫ sin nt dt over (π, 2π) = (1 − cos nπ)/n + (1 − cos nπ)/n = 2(1 − cos nπ)/n.
(a) For odd n, cos nπ = −1, so ⟨f, sin nt⟩ = 4/n and cₙ = 4/(nπ). For even n, cos nπ = 1, so cₙ = 0.
(b) Term n carries cₙ²Kₙ = 16/(n²π²) × π = 16/(n²π); the table keeps a running total and subtracts it from E = 2π.
(c) The term n = 1 carries 81.06 %; adding n = 3 brings the total to 90.06 %. Two nonzero terms carry 90 % of the energy.
(d) Σ cₙ²Kₙ = Σ 16/(n²π) over odd n = (16/π)(π²/8) = 2π, which equals E. The error energy falls towards zero, as completeness promises.
examples.answer: cₙ = 4/(nπ) for odd n and 0 for even n; the terms n = 1 and 3 carry 90.06 % of the energy 2π; Σ 16/(n²π) over odd n = 2π = E.

examples.question: On 0 ≤ t ≤ 1 expand x(t) = t² in the shifted Legendre set φ₁ = 1, φ₂ = 2t − 1, φ₃ = 6t² − 6t + 1, with K₁ = 1, K₂ = 1/3, K₃ = 1/5. Find the coefficients, the error energy after two and after three terms, and check Parseval's relation.
steps: Energy of x: E = ∫₀¹ t⁴ dt = 1/5 = 0.2.
Error energy after two terms: 1/5 − 1/9 − 1/12 = 1/180 ≈ 0.00556, about 2.8 % of E. After three terms: 1/180 − 1/180 = 0.
examples.answer: c₁ = 1/3, c₂ = 1/2, c₃ = 1/6; error energy 1/180 ≈ 0.0056 after two terms and 0 after three; 1/9 + 1/12 + 1/180 = 1/5 = E.

traps: Parseval's relation needs an orthogonal set. If ⟨φₘ, φₙ⟩ ≠ 0 the cross terms stay, and Σ |cₙ|²Kₙ is not the energy.
Multiply each |cₙ|² by Kₙ unless the set is orthonormal. For the sine set on (0, 2π), Kₙ = π; leaving it out gives Σ cₙ² = (16/π²)(π²/8) = 2 instead of the energy 2π.
Complete does not mean every finite sum is exact. The error reaches zero only in the limit: the square wave still has error energy 0.2538 after five nonzero terms.
Equality in energy is not equality at every point. At the jump t = π every sin nπ is 0, so the sine series gives 0, the midpoint of +1 and −1.

quiz.q: State Parseval's relation for a complete orthogonal set {φₙ} on [a, b].
quiz.a: ∫ₐᵇ |x(t)|² dt = Σ |cₙ|²Kₙ, with cₙ = ⟨x, φₙ⟩/Kₙ and Kₙ = ∫ₐᵇ |φₙ(t)|² dt.

quiz.q: When is an orthogonal set called complete?
quiz.a: When the error energy of the N-term approximation tends to zero as N → ∞ for every finite-energy signal on the interval; equivalently, when no nonzero signal is orthogonal to all its members.

quiz.q: Why can adding one more term of an orthogonal set never increase the error energy?
quiz.a: ε(N) = E − Σ |cₙ|²Kₙ. The new term subtracts |c|²K, which is zero or positive, and the earlier coefficients do not change.

quiz.q: An orthonormal set gives c₁ = 3, c₂ = −2 and c₃ = 1 for a signal of energy 15 on the interval. Find the error energy after these three terms. Is the signal fully represented?
quiz.a: Σ cₙ² = 9 + 4 + 1 = 14, so the error energy is 15 − 14 = 1. No: one unit of energy lies along other members of the set, or outside the set if it is not complete.

quiz.q: Use Parseval's relation for the trigonometric set to find the average power of x(t) = 4 cos(100πt) + 2 V, normalised to 1 Ω.
quiz.a: a₀ = 2 and a₁ = 4, so P = 2² + 4²/2 = 4 + 8 = 12 W, the same as the time-domain answer.

quiz.q: The set {sin nt, n = 1, 2, …} reproduces the square wave of the worked example on (0, 2π) with zero error energy in the limit. Does that make the set complete on (0, 2π)? Give a test signal.
quiz.a: No. cos t is orthogonal to every sin nt on (0, 2π), so all its coefficients are zero and the error energy stays at ∫ cos² t dt = π for every N. Completeness needs the constant and the cosines as well.

beyond: Not for the exam. The discrete cosine transform in JPEG and the wavelet bases in newer codecs are orthogonal sets chosen so that a few coefficients carry most of the energy, the bookkeeping of this chapter. Search "generalised Fourier series" and "energy compaction" to continue.
